cls: Crystalloid electrolyte solution (sodium chloride in water) - group
pharm: Fluid and electrolyte replacement / irrigation / diluent
quick: 0.9% NaCl IV titrated to fluid/electrolyte needs (e.g., 500-1000 mL boluses for resuscitation); nasal/irrigation saline as directed
Not applicable - parenteral, topical or irrigation use
Considered safe; standard isotonic fluid in pregnancy
Caution with large volumes - risk of fluid overload and hyperchloremia
Caution in cirrhosis/ascites - sodium load may worsen retention
Fluid balance, serum sodium/chloride, signs of overload; acid-base with large volumes
summary: Saline refers to a group of sodium-chloride-in-water solutions of differing concentrations used for fluid and electrolyte replacement, volume resuscitation, as a vehicle/diluent for medicines, and for irrigation or nasal/eye washing. Isotonic 0.9% sodium chloride ('normal saline') is the workhorse intravenous crystalloid; 0.45% is hypotonic, while 3% is hypertonic and used for symptomatic hyponatremia or raised intracranial pressure. Key cautions with large IV volumes are fluid overload, hypernatremia and hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. This record covers the saline group generically; specific products carry their own labeling.
indications: Restoration and maintenance of fluid and electrolyte balance (dehydration, hypovolemia)
Volume resuscitation and source-control fluid therapy
Vehicle/diluent for compatible intravenous medications and as a flush for IV lines/catheters
Hypertonic (3%) saline for symptomatic hyponatremia or raised intracranial pressure
Irrigation of wounds, body cavities, eyes, bladder; nasal saline for congestion and saline nebulisation

dosage.d: 500-1000 mL IV bolus, repeated and titrated to hemodynamic response
dosage.n: Reassess after each bolus; avoid excess in heart/renal/hepatic impairment

dosage.d: Individualised to deficits, ongoing losses and maintenance needs (e.g., approximately 25-30 mL/kg/day total fluid)
dosage.n: Account for electrolyte content; combine with other fluids as needed

dosage.d: 100-150 mL 3% NaCl IV over 10-20 min, may repeat, targeting limited sodium rise
dosage.n: Raise serum sodium no more than approximately 8-10 mmol/L in 24 h to avoid osmotic demyelination

dosage.d: Use 0.9% (or hypertonic per indication) topically/irrigation as directed; nasal sprays/drops as needed
dosage.n: Irrigation solutions are not for injection

admin: Inspect that the solution is clear and the container undamaged before use; do not use if leaking or particulate
Give isotonic saline IV via a suitable line; hypertonic (3%) saline is best given via central access and slowly to avoid phlebitis and rapid sodium shifts
Use aseptic technique; discard unused portions of single-use containers
Do not use irrigation/topical saline for injection, and do not use injectable saline beyond its single-use intent
Match the concentration to the clinical purpose (0.9% vs 0.45% vs 3%)
moa: Saline solutions provide water and sodium chloride to expand the extracellular/intravascular volume and replace electrolyte losses. Isotonic 0.9% NaCl distributes mainly into the extracellular space, supporting circulating volume; hypotonic 0.45% provides relatively more free water; hypertonic 3% raises serum osmolality and sodium, drawing water out of cells (used to correct symptomatic hyponatremia and to reduce cerebral edema). As an irrigant or diluent it provides an isotonic, physiologically compatible medium.

absolute: Conditions where added sodium or chloride is harmful for the specific concentration (e.g., hypertonic saline in hypernatremia or fluid overload)
Known clinically significant fluid overload / pulmonary edema (relative to giving more saline)
relative: Conditions with sodium/water retention (e.g., severe hypertension, preeclampsia)
monitor: Fluid balance and signs of overload (edema, raised JVP, crackles)

preg: Sodium chloride solutions are considered safe and are standard for fluid/electrolyte support in pregnancy. As with all patients, avoid excessive sodium and fluid in conditions of retention such as preeclampsia, and individualise to clinical need.
lact: Saline is compatible with breastfeeding. It contributes only sodium chloride and water and is not expected to adversely affect the breastfed infant.
renal: Use caution with large volumes in renal impairment because of the risk of fluid overload, hypernatremia and hyperchloremic acidosis. Titrate to urine output and electrolytes; reduced renal clearance limits the ability to excrete a sodium/water load.
hepatic: In hepatic cirrhosis with ascites or edema, the sodium load from saline can worsen fluid retention. Use cautiously, prefer the minimum necessary sodium, and monitor weight, edema and electrolytes.

major: No major pharmacologic drug interactions; primary concern is additive sodium/fluid load with other sodium-containing fluids or in retention states
moderate: Corticosteroids and other sodium-retaining drugs - additive fluid retention
Lithium - sodium intake affects lithium clearance (high sodium lowers, low sodium raises lithium levels)
minor: Check compatibility before mixing medications in saline (some drugs are incompatible with chloride/saline diluent)
interactions.diagnostics: Large-volume 0.9% saline can cause dilutional changes and hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis affecting electrolyte and acid-base measurements

common: Mild fluid retention / edema with larger volumes
serious: Fluid overload with pulmonary edema and heart failure
Hyponatremia or rapid sodium correction errors (with hypotonic or hypertonic use)
rare: Osmotic demyelination syndrome from over-rapid correction of hyponatremia
emergency: Acute pulmonary edema / respiratory distress from overload
Severe symptomatic sodium derangement (seizures, altered consciousness)
Osmotic demyelination from rapid sodium rise

monitoring: Fluid balance (input/output, daily weight) and clinical signs of overload
Serum sodium and chloride, and acid-base status with large or hypertonic volumes
Rate of sodium correction in hyponatremia (limit rise to about 8-10 mmol/L per 24 h)
Infusion site for phlebitis/extravasation, particularly with hypertonic saline
counsel: This is a salt-and-water solution used to keep you hydrated, replace fluids, or as a base for other medicines
Tell staff if you have heart, kidney or liver problems, as the amount may need to be limited
Report swelling, breathlessness, or pain/redness at the drip site
For nasal or eye/wound saline, follow the product directions and do not use injectable fluids for this purpose
Hypertonic (strong) saline is given carefully in hospital with blood-test monitoring
pk: Immediate intravascular volume effect on IV infusion
Volume expansion is maximal during/just after infusion (isotonic saline redistributes within about 20-30 minutes)
Not applicable - cleared by renal handling of sodium and water per physiologic state
Isotonic saline largely leaves the intravascular space within roughly 30-60 minutes (redistributes to interstitium)
Store at room temperature; protect from freezing; do not use if cloudy, leaking or past expiry; single-use containers
pearls: 'Saline' is a GROUP of sodium chloride solutions, not a single product - always specify the concentration (0.9% isotonic, 0.45% hypotonic, 3% hypertonic) and route, since each has distinct indications and hazards
Large-volume 0.9% saline causes hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis; balanced crystalloids may be preferred for big-volume resuscitation in many settings
Correct symptomatic hyponatremia with 3% saline but limit the sodium rise to about 8-10 mmol/L per 24 h to avoid osmotic demyelination
Give hypertonic saline cautiously, ideally via central access, to avoid phlebitis and extravasation injury
Use the smallest necessary sodium/fluid load in heart failure, renal failure and cirrhosis; reassess volume status frequently
missed: Not applicable - saline is administered or used as clinically indicated rather than on a fixed self-dosing schedule. For maintenance infusions, the rate is adjusted by the care team rather than 'made up' if interrupted.
overdose: Excessive administration causes fluid overload (pulmonary edema, heart failure), hypernatremia and hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis; over-rapid hypertonic saline can cause dangerous sodium derangement and osmotic demyelination. Management is to stop or slow the infusion, restrict sodium and fluid, give diuretics for overload, correct electrolytes and acid-base carefully, and provide supportive care with close monitoring.
